newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Patchy European cocoa grinds belie solid demand.
newsitem.headline: Patchy European cocoa grinds belie solid demand.

text.p: At first glance European cocoa consumption in the fourth quarter look to be patchy at best but analysts said underlying demand remained strong and lower UK and German grinds merely reflected shifts in processing.
"There has been an increase in consumption but it has not really been reflected in the European grinds," one analyst said.
Analysts identified a major factor -- the shift in processing capacity back to origin countries such as the Ivory Coast and Indonesia, something that will impact more in 1997.

Only the Dutch grind, the world's biggest, came out ahead in the fourth quarter, rising a modest 3.9 percent to 97,273 tonnes of beans from the same period in 1995. It was only slightly below anlaysts' predictions of five percent growth.
The UK grind, hit by a slowdown at a Mars processing plant, dropped by 3.3 percent to 45,147 tonnes, largely in line with industry forecasts.
But the German grind was a surprise, dropping in the fourth quarter by 21.2 percent to 56,255 tonnes as major processor Hamester shifted capacity between its Berlin and Hamburg plants.
"The German figure was surprising but that could be a blip. The totals for 1996 are more representative," the analyst added.
Looking at the year totals -- the Netherlands was up nine percent to 388,412 tonnes, Germany down three percent to 251,069 tonnes and the UK grind up 18.5 percent at 189,037 tonnes.
A further indication of solid demand came from Britain's Cadbury this week, announcing a review which showed a five percent jump in 1996 UK confectionery sales to a record 4.9 billion sterling.
Analysts said the figures showed demand was intact, although they added the scope for grind growth in Europe was limited.

The latest French import statistics bore this out -- monthly bean imports dropping year on year in October 1996 to 9,131 from 9,752 tonnes and the Jan/Oct figure roughly flat 99,709 tonnes against 97,267 in the same period in 1995.
"Two years ago we saw an increase in French and Italian grinds but that has now stabilised and we won't see any further increases there," an analyst noted.
Dutch industry sources expect processing in the Netherlands will remain strong but they add this year's near ten percent full-year rise will be hard to achieve in 1997.
Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association (NCV), predicts some 400,000 tonnes of beans will be processed in the Netherlands in the current 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) season.

But grindings elsewhere in Europe could be under pressure through 1997, affected by increasing capacity at origin, as the big European processors look for cost savings in a business that has seen margins eroded over the past few years.

"We will see good demand in 1997 but that will not be reflected in European grindings. The extra capcity will all come from origin," one analyst commented, saying the Ivory Coast, Indonesia and Ghana would be the main centres involved.
"The whole grind figure for Europe could be flat or even fall through next year," he predicted.
He declined to put a precise figure on origin output but said local output could add 1.5/2.0 percent to the world grind.
